description: Structures, unions, enum, typedef and dynamic memory allocation in C

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to define a structure in C?
questions.explanation: The struct keyword is used to define a structure in C.

questions.questionText: Which is the correct declaration of a structure variable?
questions.explanation: If Student is a structure tag, struct Student s1; declares s1 as a variable of that structure type.

questions.questionText: Which operator is used to access a structure member using a structure variable?
questions.explanation: The dot operator is used to access members through a structure variable.

questions.questionText: Which operator is used to access a structure member through a pointer to the structure?
questions.explanation: The arrow operator -> is used when accessing a structure member through a pointer.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? struct Student { int age; }; int main() { struct Student s = {20}; printf("%d", s.age); }
questions.explanation: The structure variable s is initialized with age equal to 20.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between a structure and a union in C?
questions.optionB: Union members share the same memory location
questions.explanation: Members of a union share the same memory location, while structure members generally have separate storage.

questions.questionText: In a union, at a given time, which member can generally hold a meaningful value?
questions.optionC: The member whose value was most recently stored, subject to type and access rules
questions.explanation: Union members overlap in storage, so storing a value in one member affects the shared storage.

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to define a union?
questions.explanation: The union keyword is used to define a union type.

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to define an enumeration in C?
questions.explanation: The enum keyword is used to define an enumeration.

questions.questionText: What is the default value of the first enumerator if no value is specified?
questions.explanation: The first enumerator has value 0 by default.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; int main() { printf("%d", GREEN); }
questions.explanation: By default, RED is 0, GREEN is 1 and BLUE is 2.

questions.questionText: Which keyword creates an alternative name for an existing type?
questions.explanation: typedef creates an alternative name, or alias, for an existing type.

questions.questionText: What does the following statement do? typedef unsigned int uint;
questions.optionB: Creates uint as an alias for unsigned int
questions.optionC: Creates a new integer data type in memory
questions.explanation: The statement makes uint an alias for unsigned int.

questions.questionText: Which header file declares malloc(), calloc(), realloc() and free()?
questions.explanation: The standard dynamic memory allocation functions are declared in stdlib.h.

questions.questionText: Which function is used to allocate a block of memory dynamically?
questions.explanation: malloc() allocates a specified number of bytes of uninitialized memory.

questions.questionText: What does malloc() return on successful allocation?
questions.optionB: A pointer to the allocated memory
questions.explanation: malloc() returns a pointer to the allocated memory on success and NULL if allocation fails.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between malloc() and calloc()?
questions.optionB: calloc() initializes allocated bytes to zero
questions.explanation: calloc() allocates memory for multiple elements and initializes all bits of the allocated storage to zero.

questions.questionText: Which function is used to resize previously allocated dynamic memory?
questions.explanation: realloc() changes the size of a previously allocated memory block.

questions.questionText: Which function releases dynamically allocated memory?
questions.explanation: free() releases memory previously allocated dynamically.

questions.questionText: What is a memory leak?
questions.optionB: Failing to release dynamically allocated memory when it is no longer needed
questions.explanation: A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory is no longer reachable or needed but has not been released.

questions.questionText: What will be the output? int *p = malloc(sizeof(int)); if(p != NULL) { *p = 25; printf("%d", *p); free(p); }
questions.explanation: If allocation succeeds, 25 is stored in the allocated memory and then printed.

questions.questionText: What is the size of a structure determined by?
questions.optionB: The combined storage requirements of its members plus possible padding and alignment
questions.optionC: Only the size of its largest member
questions.explanation: The size of a structure includes its members and may include padding inserted for alignment.

questions.questionText: What is the size of a union generally related to?
questions.optionA: The sum of all member sizes
questions.optionB: The size required for its largest member, plus any required alignment
questions.explanation: Union members share storage, so the union generally needs enough space for its largest member, subject to alignment.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of sizeof() when allocating memory dynamically?
questions.optionA: To determine the required number of bytes for a type
questions.explanation: sizeof() can be used to determine the number of bytes required for a type, making dynamic allocation expressions more portable.

questions.questionText: Which statement is safest when using malloc() for an array of n integers?
questions.explanation: n * sizeof(int) requests enough bytes for n integer objects.
